title: What Is Arcjet AI Security? How It Works (2026 Guide)
summary: What is Arcjet AI security—a runtime protection check inside your application, not a gateway or filter. It clarifies where protection occurs.
body_markdown:
## Where Arcjet AI security excels and falls short


Arcjet's design gives it real advantages over gateways and model-side filters. Because it's **a new product with no outside testing** , treat those advantages as claims until you have run it yourself. This assessment rests on the maker's pages and design, and we haven't run it.


### Arcjet AI security strengths from its in-code design


The usual alternative is scattered if-statements nobody reviews, wired into agents by hand. Arcjet replaces that with a check inside your own code, so it sees the same request, user and tool call your application sees. A gateway sitting upstream sees only traffic, not intent.


Placement also dictates reach. Arcjet's documentation lists 20 agent integrations, 13 frameworks and only 3 languages.


That's broad coverage of the agent tooling people actually use, so adoption is a library import, not a new network hop. But three languages means a team on any other stack finds no documented path in.


Activepieces has no native Arcjet integration, but it covers part of that gap.


Its open source monorepo holds 747 integrations in packages/integrations/community, and each integration's action is a single definition that runs as a flow step and is also exposed as a tool schema on the per-project MCP server, which eliminates the need to implement the integration twice, as the Integrations Framework and MCP Server documentation lay out, so developers rarely need to build service integrations from scratch.


That same action is reachable from Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or an agent you built, with no second integration. A check service you host and call from an HTTP request step sits in the flow the same way every other connector does.


### Arcjet AI security gaps and unknowns


It's young, and the docs describe what it should do, not what independent testers have measured. The wider picture is still thin. The[Blue Radius](https://blueradius.io/research/ai-agent-incident-tracker) tracker's documented agent cases moved from 41 to 34, while those confirmed as real-world incidents rose from 7 to 11.


Fewer cases overall but more of them real suggests the field is **shifting from hypothetical attacks to live ones** . The sample is also small, so no one can yet say how often a runtime guard would have stopped one.


That leaves the limits the docs themselves state. It also leaves everything we can't know without a trial: false positives on your traffic, added latency, and how it behaves against an attack nobody has catalogued. A pilot on one low-risk agent would answer those.
